fetched_contents.text: Innate immunity in vertebrates: an overview Summary Innate immunity is a semi‐specific and widely distributed form of immunity, which represents the first line of defence against pathogens. This type of immunity is critical to maintain homeostasis and prevent microbe invasion, eliminating a great variety of pathogens and contributing with the activation of the adaptive immune response. The components of innate immunity include physical and chemical barriers, humoral and cell‐mediated components, which are present in all jawed vertebrates. The understanding of innate defence mechanisms in non‐mammalian vertebrates is the key to comprehend the general picture of vertebrate innate immunity and its evolutionary history. This is also essential for the identification of new molecules with applications in immunopharmacology and immunotherapy. In this review, we describe and discuss the main elements of vertebrate innate immunity, presenting core findings in this field and identifying areas that need further investigation. Keywords: defence mechanisms, evolutionary history, infection, innate immunity, vertebrates ---------------------------------------- Abbreviations AMP antimicrobial peptide APP acute phase protein CRP C‐reactive protein FV3 frog virus 3 IFN interferon IL interleukin ITL intraepithelial lymphocyte NAb natural antibody NK natural killer TGF transforming growth factor TNF tumour necrosis factor Introduction Innate immunity is defined as the first line of defence against pathogens, representing a crucial systemic response to prevent infection and maintain homeostasis.1, 2, 3 This type of immunity also has a critical role in the activation and regulation of adaptive immunity.4 Despite its constitutive elements, innate defence mechanisms have the capacity to develop an induced response during primary infection and create inflammatory conditions.5, 6 This response is specific due to the cell surface expression of pattern recognition receptors, which are capable of recognizing complex polysaccharides, glycolipids, lipoproteins, nucleotides and nucleic acids.4, 7 The elements of innate immunity include external physical barriers, humoral and cellular effector mechanisms, components that are conserved among jawed vertebrates (Table 1) with certain variations and specific characteristics.2, 3, 8 Innate immunity has been extensively studied in mammals in comparison to other vertebrates, because of its significance for human health and veterinary sciences.3, 9, 10, 11 However, a major exploration of these innate mechanisms in non‐mammalian species is essential for comprehension of the complex events involved in human innate immunity and is also crucial for the discovery of new antimicrobial, antitumour and immunomodulatory molecules with therapeutic applications. Fish host defenses against parasitic larvae rely on both recognition and control mechanisms, with innate immunity playing a central role in the earliest response. The evidence points to a recognition system that includes physical/chemical barriers, soluble factors, pattern recognition receptors, antimicrobial peptides, lysozyme, acute phase proteins, complement, cytokines, and natural antibodies, all of which are part of vertebrate innate immunity and conserved in jawed vertebrates [N1-F1]. In the context of larval parasites, the fish host must detect and limit infection early, and the evidence suggests that recognition is not limited to a single pathway but involves multiple interacting components.

The most relevant innate components to larval infection appear to be complement, lectins, soluble factors, and pattern recognition receptors, because these are highlighted as key parts of teleost innate immunity and as recognition molecules that can bind to parasite-associated molecules [N3-R1], [N3-R2], [N3-R3]. The evidence also notes that fish have both physical/chemical barriers and humoral and cell-mediated innate components, including macrophages, neutrophils, mast cells, eosinophilic granular cells, and other leukocytes, which are important for controlling infection [N1-F1]. In particular, complement and antimicrobial peptides are emphasized as major elements of innate immunity that connect innate and adaptive responses [N3-R3]. The broader fish innate-immunity review also stresses that innate immunity includes soluble factors and recognition molecules studied in the skin mucosa, which is directly relevant to larval infection routes [N3-R2].

Whether innate responses can prevent or merely delay infection depends on the parasite and the host. The evidence suggests that innate responses can eliminate parasites, but they may not always fully prevent infection. For example, the experimental evidence on fish immune responses against endoparasitic nematodes notes that encapsulation and isolation of live larvae may reduce pathology compared with excessive dead tissue, implying that innate responses can contain parasites rather than always eliminate them [N6-F3]. In addition, the fish innate-immunity overview states that innate immunity can induce responses during primary infection and create inflammatory conditions, indicating that innate defenses can change the course of infection but may not always eradicate it outright [N1-F1]. The same source also says that innate immunity is important for protecting the host from infection not only in naive fish but also after prior infection, which supports the idea that innate responses can limit reinfection or reduce severity rather than simply prevent infection [N1-F1].

Taken together, fish innate immunity against parasitic larvae is best understood as a multi-layered system that recognizes larvae through barriers, soluble factors, receptors, and leukocytes, and that these components can limit larval parasites by containment, inflammation, and clearance, but the evidence does not support a simple dichotomy between “prevention” and “delay” for all larval parasites. Instead, innate defenses often appear to reduce parasite burden or pathology while still allowing some persistence or continued infection [N1-F1], [N3-R1], [N3-R3], [N6-F3].

In vertebrate immunology, the distinction between soft and hard adaptive immunity is not cleanly separated in the provided evidence, but the available material supports a useful interpretation. The evidence frames adaptive immunity as the system that generates memory and is mediated by lymphocytes such as B and T cells, with a memory response being the basis for vaccination and secondary immunity [N1-F1], [N4-R3]. It also emphasizes that adaptive immunity is distinct from innate immunity and is centered on antigen-specific recognition by lymphocytes [N4-R3].

The evidence does not define “soft adaptive immunity” and “hard adaptive immunity” with the same precision as in some specialized immunology sources, so the safest interpretation is to treat these terms as broad conceptual contrasts rather than standard classifications. On the basis of the provided material, “hard adaptive immunity” can be interpreted as the classical, antigen-specific, memory-based response mediated by lymphocytes, including B and T cells, and involving antigen presentation, cell activation, and recall after infection [N1-F1], [N4-R3]. “Soft adaptive immunity” is not explicitly named in the evidence, but the surrounding discussion implies a more limited or less hardwired form of adaptive-like response, possibly one that is less dependent on full memory generation or that coexists with innate mechanisms [N1-F1]. The evidence also suggests that innate immunity can develop induced responses, memory-like responses, and even some form of innate immunological memory, which blurs the boundary between innate and adaptive [N1-F1].

Antigen presentation and cell activation differ substantially between the two conceptual models. In hard adaptive immunity, antigen presentation is a central process: pattern recognition receptors in innate immunity can induce an inflammatory response, but the adaptive response requires antigen-specific recognition by B and T cells, which depend on antigen presentation by antigen-presenting cells (APCs) and the production of cytokines and co-stimulatory signals [N1-F1], [N4-R3]. The evidence also notes that adaptive immunity is mediated by lymphocytes with unique receptors and that memory B and T cells are created during the primary response, supporting a hard adaptive model in which antigen presentation and activation are tightly coupled to lymphocyte specificity and memory [N4-R3], [N4-R5]. In contrast, the evidence does not provide a direct counterpart for “soft adaptive immunity,” but the broader discussion of innate immunity highlights that innate responses can be specific and can include induced responses and even memory-like behavior through epigenetic changes and cell reprogramming, which suggests a different mechanism than the fully memory-driven hard adaptive response [N1-F1]. If “soft adaptive immunity” is meant to refer to a more immediate or less memory-based form, then antigen presentation and cell activation may be less central or more broadly distributed, whereas in hard adaptive immunity they are highly specialized and require lymphocyte activation, proliferation, and memory formation [N1-F1], [N4-R3].

The immune cells and signaling pathways central to each model are also different. For hard adaptive immunity, B and T cells are central, along with lymphocytes that generate memory and the signaling pathways involved in lymphocyte activation, proliferation, and memory formation [N1-F1], [N4-R3]. The evidence also points to APCs, cytokines, and co-stimulatory signals as important for adaptive responses [N1-F1]. For soft adaptive immunity, the evidence does not provide a direct definition, so the safest inference is that it may rely more on innate-like mechanisms, such as pattern recognition receptors, cytokines, and innate immunological memory, rather than on lymphocyte memory [N1-F1]. The evidence also suggests that innate immunity can involve natural killer cells and macrophages as memory-like components, and that these provide protection in a T/B-cell-independent manner [N1-F1]. Thus, the evidence supports the idea that hard adaptive immunity is lymphocyte-mediated and memory-based, while soft adaptive immunity may be a broader, more innate-like or less memory-driven adaptive-like response that still uses antigen recognition but not necessarily full lymphocyte memory [N1-F1], [N4-R3].

In fish, adaptive immune effects on parasitic larvae are mediated primarily through T and B cell responses, but the evidence suggests that these responses are not uniform across all larval infections and can be influenced by parasite evasion, host modulation, and immune persistence. The evidence on fish B cell responses indicates that adaptive immunity is the basis for vaccination and that a memory response is the goal of effective vaccination [N4-R1]. It also states that B cells are activated, proliferate, and then secrete antibodies, which is directly relevant to mounting a response against larval antigens [N4-R4]. The evidence on fish innate and adaptive immunity further emphasizes that adaptive immunity is mediated by lymphocytes such as B and T cells, and that memory responses are created during the primary immune response [N4-R3], [N4-R5]. This supports the idea that fish T and B cell responses against larval antigens involve antigen recognition, activation, proliferation, and antibody production or cell-mediated immunity.

How T and B cell responses are mounted against larval antigens depends on the parasite and the host. The experimental evidence on fish immune responses against endoparasitic nematodes notes that both innate and adaptive responses are prominent, and that Th1 skewing toward Th2 is characteristic of antihelminthic responses in mammals, with similar patterns expected in at least some fish species [N6-F3]. It also states that various host cell receptors bind helminth molecules, triggering signal-transducing events that mobilize specific reaction patterns depending on the combination of receptors and ligands involved [N6-F3]. This suggests that T cell responses are mounted through recognition of larval antigens by receptors on host cells, with signaling pathways leading to Th1/Th2 skewing and cytokine production, while B cell responses are activated through antigen recognition and proliferation, followed by antibody secretion [N4-R4], [N6-F3]. The evidence also indicates that some fish groups may lack certain immunological elements, such as MHCII and CD4+ cells, which implies that T cell responses can vary across species and that alternative reaction pathways exist [N6-F3]. In other words, T and B cell responses are mounted against larval antigens through antigen recognition, receptor signaling, and lymphocyte activation, but the exact pathway and strength depend on the host species and parasite type.

Whether immunity becomes memory or remains local is also important. The evidence supports the idea that adaptive immunity can become memory-based. The fish B-cell evidence explicitly says that a memory response is the basis of vaccination and that B cells activate and proliferate before antibody secretion [N4-R1], [N4-R4]. The fish innate/adaptive review also notes that adaptive immunity is mediated by lymphocytes with unique receptors, and that memory B and T cells are created during the primary response [N4-R3], [N4-R5]. This suggests that, in many cases, immunity can become memory, especially in response to larval antigens that are recognized repeatedly. However, the evidence does not show that all adaptive responses become memory. The fish immune response against nematodes evidence also indicates that some fish species may have alternative pathways, and that the presence of certain immunological elements can shape the response [N6-F3]. This implies that memory can be local or broader, depending on the host and the infection.

What effects larvae have on adaptive immune persistence or suppression is a key issue. The evidence suggests that larvae can suppress or modulate adaptive immunity. The fish immune responses against nematodes review notes that antihelminthic immune strategies allow first invaders to survive for prolonged periods, whereas subsequent larval invaders face increased resistance and decreased colonization success [N6-F3]. This is consistent with a concept of concomitant immunity or immune evasion, where larvae persist because the host’s immune response is not fully effective, or because the parasite modulates the immune response to allow survival. The evidence also states that live endoparasitic larvae may be encapsulated and isolated, which can reduce pathology compared with dead tissue, but this does not necessarily mean that adaptive immunity is suppressed; rather, it suggests that the host is actively controlling the parasite through an immune response [N6-F3]. The parasite-immune response overview further notes that Th2 responses may mediate larval persistence as part of the parasite’s host-immune evasion strategy [N2-R4]. This supports the conclusion that larvae can influence adaptive immunity by promoting Th2-like responses, reducing the effectiveness of Th1 responses, and possibly allowing persistence rather than complete clearance.

Overall, T and B cell responses in fish against parasitic larvae are antigen-specific and can become memory-based, but larvae can modulate these responses through immune evasion, Th2 skewing, or persistence strategies [N4-R3], [N4-R4], [N6-F3], [N2-R4]. The evidence therefore indicates that adaptive immunity can be effective, but larvae may also suppress or alter adaptive persistence depending on the infection dynamics.

Fish host-parasite interactions involving parasitic larvae are shaped by both parasite evasion and host modulation, and the evidence points to a dynamic balance in which larvae actively subvert host immunity while hosts try to control infection through immune modulation. The evidence on monogenean-parasite interactions explicitly states that monogeneans must possess one or more immune evasion strategies, and that both innate and adaptive immune responses are mounted by fish to control parasite infection [N2-R2]. It also notes that host molecules can bind to epitopes on the parasite, sometimes acting positively on the parasite while others may act adversely [N2-F2]. This indicates that larvae do not simply passively evade immunity; they actively interact with host molecules and exploit them to survive.

The evidence also supports several specific evasion strategies. First, larvae may use host molecules to their advantage. The monogenean evidence states that host molecules can activate benign physiological processes in the parasite, while others may act adversely on monogenean integrity [N2-F2]. Second, larvae may exploit host recognition systems. The same source describes how monogenean larvae can recognize and locate the host through chemical signals, mucus, and other host factors, suggesting that larvae are not only evading immunity but also actively seeking suitable host environments [N2-F2]. Third, larvae may interfere with host recognition and attachment. The evidence notes that monogeneans are sensitive to host components and that attachment and adhesion mechanisms must fit the host epidermal architecture, otherwise parasites are dislodged [N2-F2]. This implies that larvae can modulate host attachment and microhabitat selection, which may help them avoid immune detection or reduce host clearance [N2-F2]. Fourth, larvae may interfere with immune responses. The evidence indicates that monogeneans can withstand attacks on their integrity and that some host molecules can act adversely on the parasite [N2-F2]. It also notes that the host can produce substances that bind parasite structures, but these reactions do not necessarily result in adverse effects on the parasite [N2-F2]. Taken together, these evasion strategies include host molecule exploitation, host recognition manipulation, attachment modulation, and immune interference.

Fish hosts can modulate immunity during larval infection in several ways. The evidence shows that fish produce soluble factors, recognition molecules, and effector components such as macrophages, neutrophils, mast cells, and eosinophilic granular cells [N1-F1], [N3-R2]. The monogenean evidence also states that fish can produce substances that bind parasite structures, and that these reactions can contribute to elimination of the parasites [N2-F2]. The fish immune response against nematodes evidence further indicates that both innate and adaptive responses are prominent, with Th1 skewing toward Th2 being characteristic of antihelminthic responses in mammals and likely in some fish species [N6-F3]. This suggests that hosts can modulate immunity by shifting the cytokine environment and recruiting adaptive responses. The same evidence also notes that live larvae may be encapsulated and isolated, which reduces pathology compared with dead parasite tissue, showing that hosts can actively contain and limit infection even if complete elimination is not achieved [N6-F3]. In addition, the evidence on fish immune responses against nematodes states that some fish species may lack certain immunological elements, implying that host modulation can vary by species and by the availability of immune machinery [N6-F3].

The infection outcomes associated with each immune response are mixed and depend on the balance between host defense and parasite evasion. The evidence suggests that a strong immune response can reduce parasite burden, limit pathology, and increase resistance to subsequent infections. For example, the fish immune response against nematodes evidence notes that subsequent larval invaders of the same parasite species face increased host resistance and decreased colonization success [N6-F3]. It also states that encapsulation and isolation of live larvae may reduce pathology compared with excess dead tissue, implying that effective immunity can contain infection and limit damage [N6-F3]. In contrast, larvae may also associate with persistent or chronic infection. The parasite-immune response overview notes that Th2 responses may mediate larval persistence as a host-immune evasion strategy [N2-R4], and the fish immune responses against nematodes evidence indicates that antihelminthic immune strategies allow first invaders to survive for prolonged periods [N6-F3]. This suggests that larvae can promote persistent infection when the host’s immune response is skewed or insufficiently strong.

In short, the evidence supports a model in which parasitic larvae in fish actively evade or subvert host immunity through host molecule exploitation, recognition manipulation, attachment modulation, and immune interference [N2-R2], [N2-F2], [N6-F3]. Fish hosts can modulate immunity through soluble factors, effector cells, cytokine shifts, and containment mechanisms [N1-F1], [N3-R2], [N6-F3]. The infection outcomes associated with these interactions range from reduced parasite burden and increased resistance to persistent or chronic infection, depending on the strength and specificity of the host response [N2-R4], [N6-F3]. The evidence therefore indicates that immune evasion and host modulation are central to the outcome of larval infection in fish.

It also notes that adaptive immunity is the basis for vaccination and that a memory response is what an effective vaccine aims to generate [N4-R1]. This supports a hard adaptive model in which immune cells are activated by antigen presentation, and the response becomes durable and recall-oriented.

For soft adaptive immunity, the evidence does not provide a direct definition, but it does indicate that innate immunity can develop induced responses, memory-like responses, and even some form of innate immunological memory through epigenetic changes and cell reprogramming [N1-F1]. The evidence also suggests that innate immunity includes natural killer cells and macrophages as memory-like components, which provide protection in a T/B-cell-independent manner [N1-F1]. This implies that soft adaptive immunity may be a broader, less hardwired form of adaptive-like immunity, possibly involving innate-like recognition and more immediate responses than full lymphocyte memory [N1-F1].

### 2. Antigen presentation and cell activation: how the two differ

In hard adaptive immunity, antigen presentation is central. The evidence emphasizes that adaptive immunity is mediated by lymphocytes such as B and T cells and that antigen presentation is required for lymphocyte activation and memory formation [N1-F1], [N4-R3]. The fish immune response against nematodes evidence also notes that various host cell receptors bind helminth molecules, triggering signal-transducing events that mobilize specific reaction patterns depending on the combination of receptors and ligands involved [N6-F3]. This supports a hard adaptive mechanism in which antigen recognition and presentation drive lymphocyte activation and recall.

In contrast, the evidence does not provide a direct counterpart for soft adaptive immunity, but the broader discussion of innate immunity suggests that antigen presentation and cell activation may be less central or more broadly distributed in a softer form. The evidence indicates that innate immunity can be specific and can include induced responses and memory-like behavior, even though it does not rely on lymphocyte memory in the same way [N1-F1]. This suggests that soft adaptive immunity may involve pattern recognition receptors and other innate-like mechanisms, with activation being more distributed across innate and adaptive components rather than confined to lymphocytes [N1-F1], [N4-R3].

### 3. Central immune cells and signaling pathways

For hard adaptive immunity, the central immune cells are B and T cells, along with antigen-presenting cells and the signaling pathways that support lymphocyte activation, proliferation, and memory formation [N1-F1], [N4-R3]. The evidence also points to cytokines and co-stimulatory signals as important for adaptive responses [N1-F1]. In fish, B-cell responses are activated, proliferate, and then secrete antibodies, which is directly relevant to mounting a response against larval antigens [N4-R4].

For soft adaptive immunity, the evidence does not provide a direct definition, but it does point to innate immunity as a broader system that includes natural killer cells, macrophages, and other cells that can show memory-like behavior [N1-F1]. This suggests that the signaling pathways central to soft adaptive immunity may be more innate-like, involving pattern recognition receptors, cytokines, and epigenetic reprogramming rather than full lymphocyte memory [N1-F1], [N4-R3].

### 4. Effects on parasitic larvae in fish

In fish, adaptive immune effects on parasitic larvae are mediated primarily through T and B cell responses, but the evidence indicates that these responses are not uniform across all larval infections. The evidence on fish B-cell responses indicates that B cells are activated, proliferate, and then secrete antibodies, which is directly relevant to mounting a response against larval antigens [N4-R4]. The evidence also states that adaptive immunity is mediated by lymphocytes such as B and T cells, and that memory responses are created during the primary immune response [N4-R3], [N4-R5]. This supports the idea that fish T and B cell responses against larval antigens involve antigen recognition, activation, proliferation, and antibody production or cell-mediated immunity.

However, larvae can influence these responses in several ways. The evidence suggests that larvae can suppress or modulate adaptive immunity. The fish immune responses against nematodes review notes that antihelminthic immune strategies allow first invaders to survive for prolonged periods, whereas subsequent larval invaders face increased resistance and decreased colonization success [N6-F3]. It also states that live endoparasitic larvae may be encapsulated and isolated, which can reduce pathology compared with excess dead tissue, implying that the host is actively controlling the parasite through an immune response [N6-F3]. The parasite-immune response overview further notes that Th2 responses may mediate larval persistence as part of the parasite’s host-immune evasion strategy [N2-R4]. Taken together, these findings indicate that larvae can shape the adaptive response by promoting Th2-like responses, reducing the effectiveness of Th1 responses, and allowing persistence rather than complete clearance [N6-F3], [N2-R4].

### 5. Memory versus local persistence

Whether immunity becomes memory or remains local is an important distinction. The evidence supports the idea that adaptive immunity can become memory-based. The fish B-cell evidence explicitly says that a memory response is the basis of vaccination and that B cells activate and proliferate before antibody secretion [N4-R1], [N4-R4]. The fish innate/adaptive review also notes that memory B and T cells are created during the primary response [N4-R3], [N4-R5]. This suggests that, in many cases, immunity can become memory, especially in response to larval antigens that are recognized repeatedly.

However, the evidence also shows that adaptive responses can remain local or be less durable. The fish immune response against nematodes evidence indicates that some fish species may lack certain immunological elements, such as MHCII and CD4+ cells, which implies that T cell responses can vary across species and that alternative reaction pathways exist [N6-F3]. This means that memory is not guaranteed, and immunity may remain local depending on the host and parasite type.

### 6. Parasite evasion, host modulation, and infection outcomes

Fish host-parasite interactions involving parasitic larvae are shaped by both parasite evasion and host modulation. The evidence on monogenean-parasite interactions explicitly states that monogeneans must possess one or more immune evasion strategies, and that both innate and adaptive immune responses are mounted by fish to control parasite infection [N2-R2]. It also notes that host molecules can bind to epitopes on the parasite, sometimes acting positively on the parasite while others may act adversely [N2-F2]. This indicates that larvae do not simply passively evade immunity; they actively interact with host molecules and exploit them to survive.

The evidence supports several specific evasion strategies. First, larvae may use host molecules to their advantage. Host molecules can activate benign physiological processes in the parasite while others may act adversely on monogenean integrity [N2-F2]. Second, larvae may exploit host recognition systems. The evidence describes how monogenean larvae can recognize and locate the host through chemical signals, mucus, and other host factors, suggesting that larvae are not only evading immunity but also actively seeking suitable host environments [N2-F2]. Third, larvae may interfere with host recognition and attachment. The evidence notes that monogeneans are sensitive to host components and that attachment and adhesion mechanisms must fit the host epidermal architecture, otherwise parasites are dislodged [N2-F2]. Fourth, larvae may interfere with immune responses. The evidence indicates that monogeneans can withstand attacks on their integrity and that some host molecules can act adversely on the parasite [N2-F2]. It also notes that fish can produce substances that bind parasite structures, but these reactions do not necessarily result in adverse effects on the parasite [N2-F2]. Taken together, these evasion strategies include host molecule exploitation, recognition manipulation, attachment modulation, and immune interference [N2-R2], [N2-F2], [N6-F3].

Fish hosts can modulate immunity during larval infection in several ways. The evidence shows that fish produce soluble factors, recognition molecules, and effector components such as macrophages, neutrophils, mast cells, and eosinophilic granular cells [N1-F1], [N3-R2]. The monogenean evidence also states that fish can produce substances that bind parasite structures, and that these reactions can contribute to elimination of the parasites [N2-F2]. The fish immune response against nematodes evidence further indicates that both innate and adaptive responses are prominent, with Th1 skewing toward Th2 being characteristic of antihelminthic responses in mammals and likely in some fish species [N6-F3]. This suggests that hosts can modulate immunity by shifting the cytokine environment and recruiting adaptive responses. The same evidence also notes that live larvae may be encapsulated and isolated, which reduces pathology compared with dead parasite tissue, showing that hosts can actively contain and limit infection even if complete elimination is not achieved [N6-F3].

The infection outcomes associated with these interactions range from reduced parasite burden and increased resistance to persistent or chronic infection. The evidence suggests that a strong immune response can reduce parasite burden, limit pathology, and increase resistance to subsequent infections. For example, the fish immune response against nematodes evidence notes that subsequent larval invaders of the same parasite species face increased host resistance and decreased colonization success [N6-F3]. It also states that encapsulation and isolation of live larvae may reduce pathology compared with excess dead tissue, implying that effective immunity can contain infection and limit damage [N6-F3]. In contrast, larvae may also associate with persistent or chronic infection. The parasite-immune response overview notes that Th2 responses may mediate larval persistence as a host-immune evasion strategy [N2-R4], and the fish immune responses against nematodes evidence indicates that antihelminthic immune strategies allow first invaders to survive for prolonged periods [N6-F3]. This suggests that larvae can promote persistent infection when the host’s immune response is skewed or insufficiently strong [N2-R4], [N6-F3].

### 7. Integrated conclusion

In fish, hard adaptive immunity is the classical, antigen-specific, memory-based response mediated by B and T cells, with antigen presentation and cell activation being central to lymphocyte activation, proliferation, and memory formation [N1-F1], [N4-R3]. Soft adaptive immunity, by contrast, is not clearly defined in the evidence, but it appears to represent a broader, more immediate, or less memory-driven adaptive-like response that may rely more on innate-like recognition and signaling pathways rather than full lymphocyte memory [N1-F1]. In practice, the evidence suggests that fish adaptive immunity against parasitic larvae is effective but highly variable: it can become memory-based, can be influenced by larvae through immune evasion and Th2 skewing, and can lead to reduced parasite burden and resistance in some cases, while also allowing persistence in others [N4-R3], [N4-R4], [N6-F3], [N2-R4].

Overall, the fish host response to parasitic larvae is a dynamic interplay between innate defenses, adaptive immunity, parasite evasion, and host modulation, with hard adaptive immunity providing durable memory and recall, while soft adaptive immunity may represent a more flexible or immediate adaptive-like response that still operates within the broader immune system [N1-F1], [N4-R3], [N2-F2], [N6-F3].
